text: We were obsessed with reducing friction, this was our constant battle.
speaker: Maya Prohovnik
context: Maya is sharing an early Anchor story about how they solved podcast distribution challenges. At the time, distributing podcasts to platforms like Apple Podcasts was extremely technical and difficult for creators - requiring Apple IDs, understanding RSS feeds, and dealing with technical hurdles. Maya explains how they created what appeared to be an automated solution by having college interns manually handle all the technical distribution work behind the scenes, making it feel seamless for users.
text_ko: 우리는 마찰(friction)을 줄이는 데 집착했어요. 그건 늘 우리가 싸워온 문제였어요.
text_zh: 我们一直在琢磨怎么把摩擦降到最低，这几乎成了我们的一场持久战。
text_es: Estábamos obsesionados con reducir la fricción; era una batalla constante.
key_sentence: We were obsessed with reducing friction, this was our constant battle.
original_text: We were obsessed with reducing friction, this was our constant battle. And so we hired a couple of college interns and we brought them in and we were like, people are going to push this magical one button in the Anchor app and they're going to say, I want to distribute my podcast, and your job is going to be to do all that same manual stuff manually, but to them it's going to feel magical and it happened automatically.

vocabulary.definition: The process of minimizing obstacles or difficulties that hinder progress or efficiency.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and technology, reducing friction often refers to streamlining processes to enhance user experience and operational efficiency.
vocabulary.nuance: This phrase conveys a proactive approach to problem-solving and is often used in discussions about improving customer interactions or internal workflows.

vocabulary.definition: Having an intense preoccupation or fixation on a particular idea, goal, or task.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, being obsessed often implies a deep commitment to achieving excellence or innovation, sometimes at the expense of other priorities.
vocabulary.nuance: While it can indicate passion and dedication, it may also suggest an unhealthy level of focus that could lead to burnout or neglect of other important areas.

vocabulary.definition: An ongoing struggle or challenge that requires continuous effort to overcome.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the corporate world, a constant battle may refer to the relentless competition in the market or the ongoing efforts to improve processes and meet customer demands.
vocabulary.nuance: This phrase often carries a connotation of persistence and resilience, highlighting the challenges faced in achieving goals.

text: I think data is amazing and I'm like, we have such an incredible insights team at Spotify, both my insights team and then the broader one.
speaker: Maya Prohovnik
context: Lenny asks Maya about finding the balance between being data-driven versus gut-driven in product decisions, noting this is something many product leaders struggle with. Maya is explaining her philosophy on using data effectively while warning against over-reliance on data alone. She advocates for using data as one input among many in the creative product development process rather than as the sole decision-making framework.
text_ko: 데이터가 정말 대단하다고 생각해요. 스포티파이에는 제 인사이트 팀(insights team)뿐 아니라 전체 인사이트 팀도 정말 멋져요.
text_zh: 我觉得数据太棒了，我就觉得，Spotify的洞察团队（insights team）真厉害，不仅是我带的那支，整个更大的团队也都很强。
text_es: Me parece increíble lo que permiten los datos, y yo digo: tenemos un equipo de insights (insights) en Spotify impresionante, tanto mi equipo como el equipo más amplio.
key_sentence: we have such an incredible insights team at Spotify
original_text: I think data is amazing and I'm like, we have such an incredible insights team at Spotify, both my insights team and then the broader one. I think we are so lucky and we have so much knowledge about our users and different cohorts and what people need and what they're missing, and so I think that's extremely valuable. I think where people get into trouble is when they think that they can rely solely on the data.

vocabulary.definition: Deep understandings or realizations derived from data analysis that can inform decision-making and strategy.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, insights are critical for identifying trends, understanding customer behavior, and making informed strategic choices.
vocabulary.nuance: Insights often carry a connotation of being actionable and valuable, distinguishing them from mere data or information.

text: I think something that I've had to learn is that being gut driven isn't the same as just saying to people, I told you or I believe this, so you have to do it. There really is an art I think to balancing that.
speaker: Maya Prohovnik
context: Maya continues discussing how to balance gut instinct with data in product decisions, specifically addressing the challenge of leading in a large organization. She's explaining how being gut-driven requires more sophistication when you need to influence many stakeholders who aren't on your immediate team. Maya emphasizes that gut instinct must be communicated with objective reasoning and supporting evidence to be effective in larger organizational contexts.
text_ko: 제가 배워야 했던 것 중 하나는, 직감에 이끌려 행동하는 것(gut driven)이 단순히 사람들에게 '내가 말했잖아'라거나 '내가 이렇다고 믿으니까 네가 그렇게 해야 해'라고 말하는 것과 같지 않다는 거예요. 그걸 균형 있게 맞추는 건 정말 요령이 필요해요.
text_zh: 我后来学到的一点是，凭直觉做决定和回头跟别人说“我早就说过”或“我觉得应该这样，你们就得照做”不是一回事。要在这两者之间找到平衡，确实挺讲究拿捏的。
text_es: Creo que algo que he tenido que aprender es que dejarse guiar por el instinto no es lo mismo que simplemente decirle a la gente "te lo dije" o "yo creo esto, así que tienen que hacerlo". Encontrar ese equilibrio es todo un arte, creo.
key_sentence: There really is an art to explaining gut feelings as objectively as possible.
original_text: I think something that I've had to learn is that being gut driven isn't the same as just saying to people, I told you or I believe this, so you have to do it. There really is an art I think to balancing that. And I think that what I try to do is always still as objectively as possible explain why my gut is feeling that way.

vocabulary.definition: The act of maintaining equilibrium between different elements or factors.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, balancing often refers to managing competing priorities, such as cost versus quality or short-term gains versus long-term sustainability.
vocabulary.nuance: This term implies a careful consideration of multiple factors rather than a simple choice, making it suitable for discussions about strategy and decision-making.

vocabulary.definition: A skill or craft that requires creativity and practice, often associated with aesthetic value or expression.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, the 'art' of management or negotiation refers to the nuanced skills and creativity required to navigate complex interpersonal dynamics.
vocabulary.nuance: This term suggests that certain aspects of business are not purely technical or scientific but require a creative and subjective approach.

vocabulary.definition: Being motivated or compelled by a strong desire or ambition to achieve a goal.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the corporate environment, a 'driven' individual is often seen as someone who is proactive, ambitious, and focused on achieving results.
vocabulary.nuance: While being driven is generally viewed positively, it can also imply a relentless pursuit that may overlook collaboration or team dynamics.

text: you really have to be able to tell the signal through the noise... we want to be building for the 80%, and even though the 20% are going to be more vocal, that's just going to get you deeper into that hole.
speaker: Maya Prohovnik
context: Lenny asks Maya about the difficult decision to change Anchor from version 1.0 to 2.0 despite having users who loved the existing product. Maya is explaining the challenge of making strategic product decisions when you have satisfied but vocal users who represent a minority. She's describing how they learned to distinguish between feedback from power users versus the broader market they wanted to serve, emphasizing the importance of building for mainstream adoption rather than just the most engaged current users.
text_ko: 노이즈(noise) 속에서 진짜 신호(signal)를 골라낼 줄 알아야 해요. 우리는 사용자 80%를 위해 제품을 만들고 싶어요. 20%가 더 목소리를 낼 수는 있지만, 그들만 좇다 보면 오히려 더 깊은 수렁에 빠지게 돼요.
text_zh: 你得能在噪音里分辨出真正的信号（signal through the noise）。我们要把精力放在那80%上（build for the 80%），虽然那20%会更会发声，但跟着他们走只会让你越陷越深。
text_es: Hay que saber separar la señal del ruido. Queremos construir pensando en el 80% y, aunque el 20% vaya a ser más vocal, eso solo nos va a hundir más en ese agujero.
key_sentence: You must tell the signal through the noise, not just build for the vocal 20%.
original_text: I think you really have to be able to tell the signal through the noise, and even if you've got lots of vocal users asking for something, we used to have this rule, the 80/20 rule, where it's like you can't just build for that 20, I don't think we made this up by the way. I think this is a common thing, but we'd always refer to it and say, we want to be building for the 80%, and even though the 20% are going to be more vocal, that's just going to get you deeper into that hole of that problem of you're not really building for everyone.

vocabulary.definition: The ability to identify important information amidst irrelevant or distracting data.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and technology, this phrase is often used to emphasize the importance of focusing on key metrics or insights that drive decision-making, rather than getting lost in overwhelming amounts of data.
vocabulary.nuance: This phrase suggests a need for discernment and clarity, often used in discussions about data analysis or market research.

vocabulary.definition: Designing products or services primarily to meet the needs of the majority of users, rather than catering to a small, niche market.
vocabulary.businessContext: This approach is common in product development and marketing strategies, where businesses aim to create solutions that appeal to the largest segment of their target audience to maximize impact and profitability.
vocabulary.nuance: The phrase implies a focus on practicality and broad appeal, often used in contrast to catering to a vocal minority that may have specialized needs.

vocabulary.definition: Expressing opinions or concerns openly and assertively, often in a public or noticeable manner.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business setting, being vocal can refer to stakeholders, customers, or employees who actively share their feedback or criticisms, influencing company policies or product development.
vocabulary.nuance: While being vocal can be seen as positive engagement, it can also imply a tendency to dominate discussions or create conflict if not balanced with listening.

text: I think you really have to stick to it and it's really hard, but you have to keep pivoting to get to where you want to be. Kill your darlings. I love that phrase, I use it all the time.
speaker: Maya Prohovnik
context: Maya and Lenny are discussing the challenge of having a product that's working but not achieving massive scale. Maya is explaining the importance of staying committed to your larger mission and vision, even when it means making difficult decisions to change things that are currently working. She references the common creative writing advice about 'killing your darlings' - being willing to cut things you love if they don't serve the bigger picture.
text_ko: 정말 끝까지 밀고 나가야 해요. 진짜 힘들지만 원하는 곳에 가려면 계속 피벗(pivoting)해 가며 방향을 조정해야 해요. 애정 있는 아이디어도 과감히 버려야 해요 (Kill your darlings). 그 표현 정말 좋아해요, 저도 항상 써요.
text_zh: 我觉得你真的得坚持下去，虽然特别难，但你必须不断调整方向(pivot)才能到达你想要的地方。要舍得放弃心爱的项目，我特别喜欢这个说法，经常用。
text_es: Creo que realmente tienes que ser constante y es súper difícil, pero hay que seguir adaptándose para llegar donde quieres estar. Mata a tus niños bonitos (kill your darlings). Me encanta esa frase, la uso todo el tiempo.
key_sentence: You have to keep pivoting and remember to kill your darlings.

vocabulary.definition: The act of making a significant change in strategy or direction while maintaining the core vision of a project or business.
vocabulary.businessContext: In startup environments, pivoting often refers to altering a product or business model in response to market feedback or performance metrics.
vocabulary.nuance: Pivoting implies a thoughtful and strategic adjustment rather than a hasty or random change, often used in contexts where flexibility is essential for success.

text: I still don't know how many people know this.
speaker: Maya Prohovnik
context: Maya is elaborating on the earlier story about Anchor's unscalable solution for podcast distribution. She explains how they gained competitive advantage by making distribution appear automated when it was actually manual work done by interns. This created a remarkable user experience that drove word-of-mouth growth and helped them capture significant market share in podcast hosting, as competitors were offering similar technical features but without the ease-of-use advantage.
text_ko: 이걸 얼마나 많은 사람들이 알고 있는지는 아직 잘 모르겠어요.
text_zh: 我还不清楚有多少人知道这件事
text_es: Aún no sé cuánta gente está al tanto de esto.
key_sentence: I still don't know how many people know this.
original_text: I still don't know how many people know this. I think people think that we had some secret backdoor deal with Apple for distribution, but we just had college students making Apple podcast accounts and then submitting hundreds of thousands of podcasts through these accounts, and I think that was a really big part of why we got so much hosting market share so quickly because it was such an insane benefit over the other platforms which otherwise had been commoditized at that point.
